utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody in the court. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Laurie Sartorio, Anna Svensson, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Our case manager is Ms. Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too, Your Honours, and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, before you started your testimony, you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I remind you that you are still bound by that declaration. Okay? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the end of the session, I was asking you some questions about any communications between the 3rd Corps military security service and subordinate units, and my question to you is: How -- was there a system in place for sharing information? In other words, if the subordinate units' counter-intelligence operatives came into possession of information, how would that information be relayed up the chain?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. My question to you is: How would you receive information from counter-intelligence operatives from subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a communications system in place down what we termed the security line. Security organs from subordinate units, from minor units you might say, used their reports to inform the superior command on various developments. If, for example, there was an independent brigade, a brigade, it would use its reports to pass information along to its superior command, such as, for example, the division command. The division command, in turn, informed the corps command; and then the assistant commander for security attached to the corps command would receive all these reports. He would analyse the substance of these reports, and then the reports were sent on to whichever sector was concerned. Specifically, in my case, these would be reports about the kind of developments that I covered. The assistant commander for security of the corps would forward these reports to my sector; and then my superior, my boss, upon receiving such a report, would forward the document to me. This is how I learned about certain things and about activities that had to do with my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the assistant commander for security of the corps would forward these reports to my sector; and then my superior, my boss, upon receiving the report, would forward the document to me," what assistant commanders are you speaking of; and, then, please, for the record, just state who your boss is? Can we talk about particular persons here, the names?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Specifically, if a report came, for example, from the command of the 35th Division, the assistant commander for security in the corps, at the time discussed yesterday, 1994 and 1995, was Major Pavel [as interpreted] Imamovic. He received certain reports and forwarded those to the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps command, Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic. Then, in mid-1995, he was replaced by Colonel Agan Haseljic. Whenever they received those reports from someone from one those units, if this report contained any information that had a bearing on my work in the counter-intelligence sector, this document would be forwarded to my sector. Major Osman Vlajcic was the head of my sector. He would study the report and then he would address it to whoever was concerned, and that was normally one of us, the operatives working there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. There's something I would like to understand here. Maybe, at lines 23 to 25, the witness says things would be received from the 35th Division and the assistant commander for security in the corps, at the time discussed, was Major Pavel Imamovic." Then he said he received certain reports and forwarded those to the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps, which is Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic. It looks like this position is occupied by two persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I was going to clarify that, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, can you repeat the first name of Mr. Imamovic, because I believe the record is incorrect. What is his first name again?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that. Fadil, Fadil Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, what the Judge is asking is also my confusion when you say the assistant commander for security in the corps received certain reports and forwarded them to the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps. When you say "assistant commander for security in the corps," do you mean in a subordinate division? How are you using the word "corps" here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There cannot be a subordinate division that is a corps. It either comes from a division or a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand that, and that's why I'm asking him to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then you are confusing the question by saying "subordinate division." What do you mean by "the corps" here, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You may answer the Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me make one thing clear. I'm not a professional military man. I happened to be a member of that military unit at the time, that is true, but there are certain limits to my understanding of how this worked. The corps is an organisational unit comprising several subordinate, smaller units: Brigades - independent units, that is - battalions, and divisions. As for the chain of command, it looks like some sort of a pyramid, and then the corps is at the top of this pyramid. Above the corps in the system of command and control, or in the organisational chart as far as I can remember, at the time we only had the Main Staff. There was the subordinate unit, the 35th Division, and there was the corps command. The subordinate division, the 35th Division, also had its own subordinate units which received reports down the security line of command, send them down to the division, and the division up to the corps. When these reached the head of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I please interrupt you. Let me ask the question differently. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to interrupt. Just going back to the answer of the witness, which appears to have caused the confusion, I've been informed by my colleague that the answer made perfect sense, but, unfortunately, it hasn't been recorded in the transcript correctly. So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's try and correct that. That's what we're trying to do. Now, sir, who was the assistant commander for security in the 3rd Corps, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time we are discussing, the assistant commander for security in the 3rd Corps was Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And what position at that time did Fadil Imamovic occupy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, at the time Major Fadil Imamovic was assistant commander for security in the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clears the question up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, what was the -- was there a major source for you of your -- for your counter-intelligence information? Where did you get your information from?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally gathered intelligence in several different ways. For the most part, I would obtain information the following way: By talking to any prisoners, to civilians who were exchanged by the other side, by collating information from reports received from subordinate units in the way I just described a minute ago, and based on information that I obtained from my sources in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So one of your sources would be POWs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how would you be informed about the existence of a POW?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, talking about this segment, I had the brief in the counter-intelligence sector that I talked about yesterday. Activities of the Serb-Montenegrin aggressor - that's how we defined my brief - and all activities to do with the work of that sector were passed on to me. Among other things, as a result of the fighting, certain people were captured along the front lines, and those people were POWs. I spoke to these persons, and this was one way for me to retrieve certain types of information that was material, especially to units who needed this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But my specific question for you is this: When someone became a POW, how would you learn about this? Who would tell you, and how soon after someone became a POW would you learn this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain how it worked in practice in my case. We had meetings on a daily basis within our sector, the counter-intelligence sector. My boss, Major Osman Vlajcic, briefed us every morning and handed out assignments to all of us. There were a total of five of us operatives working there. It would sometimes be the case at one of these morning briefings that he would, for example, say he had information indicating that there were a certain number of POWs, one or more, who were to be brought into the POW Reception Centre in Zenica. His information, for example, indicated that these persons had been captured in a combat zone where there was fighting going on at a particular point in time. All this was probably - certainly, actually - based on some sort of a written report. Whichever unit was engaged in combat in a certain area took these prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how soon after you received this information would you want to interview the POW?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted interviews the minute I was told that a certain POW was brought in, and once they were put up in the POW Reception Centre in Zenica. Normally, this would happen after a POW had been brought over from the area of responsibility of that particular unit and over to the centre. It would sometimes be the case that a unit involved in the fighting, a unit taking a prisoner -- I'm sorry. Security organs of that particular unit in the area of responsibility of that unit, in their HQ, would first talk to these prisoners. They would obtain information that seemed important at the time. Information that the unit in question had found much more useful than any information I could have retrieved several days after. The moment this person was captured, any information provided was far more important than any additional information that could have followed up three or four days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Exactly. So when a POW was captured, where was that POW -- were there procedures in place for where that POW was supposed to be brought to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, at the time, yes, there was a procedure. Efforts were made for each POW to be brought in as quickly as possible to the POW Reception Centre in Zenica. I'm talking about the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps specifically. This is the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. Once all these activities were performed, the ones I mentioned a while ago, efforts were made for these POWs to be brought in as quickly as possible. Of course, they would be listed in keeping with the Geneva Conventions. They would be registered with the International Red Cross, and put up in the POW Reception Centre in Zenica. I can't say exactly whether it took a single day, two, or more. Every effort was made to do this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I would like to move on to the topic -- another topic. I believe that you mentioned, earlier in your testimony, African or Asian -- persons who came from African or Asian countries, and my question to you is: When is the first time that you learned of these persons? I believe I asked you also if they were known under another term, and you said "Mujahedin." So my question is: When is the first time you learned about the existence of a Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally learned about the existence of the Mujahedin sometime in 1993, I believe. Unofficially or semi-officially, this was the story circulating among the common folk. Likewise, you could hear these stories among the ranks of the army. Nothing special, just something to the effect that there were people called "the Mujahedin" fighting for the BH Army. This was the sort of story one could hear at the time. This is what I heard. Officially, having started work with the counter-intelligence sector, I want to point out again that my boss was Major Osman Vlajcic who was personally in charge of monitoring any activities to do with this Afro-Asian element, the Mujahedin. So it wasn't before then that I knew for sure, and I knew that he was involved with this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about them?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the code of conduct that we followed in that particular unit was to each mind our own business. No ill intention, but nobody was to interfere with anyone else's work or with anyone else's brief. There was no need for me to do anything like that, since this was his brief. This was something that he did. He didn't need to share anything, and he never shared anything. I, myself, didn't pry, because I had my own brief. It was quite a comprehensive one, and I was quite busy. His brief was no concern of mine at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know exactly, more or less, when it was that he told you about the existence of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I joined the sector, I believe, sometime in September 1994. There were those regular morning briefings that I mentioned. It was there that I learned, with any degree of certainty, that this, in fact, existed and that he was the person in charge of monitoring this. My boss, Major Osman Vlajcic, he was in charge of, well, monitoring these, what shall I call them, activities that they performed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question, really, is: Do you know more or less when? Month, date, year? When did you first come to know of their existence officially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Officially, I learned, as I said, sometime in September 1994, at one of the morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you ever discuss the Mujahedin with your colleagues; and if so, what were the discussions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the witness has fully dealt with this question that's just been put. He said earlier that there was a code of conduct and this witness didn't pry into what others were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think I'm asking a different question, Your Honour. I'm not asking about whether he participated in any work with them. I'm asking if he ever discussed the Mujahedin, just in general, with the colleagues; and if so, what were the stories about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered the question to some extent. Specifically, off the record, there was precious little that one actually knew, and it wasn't official information. We each tried to abide by the code that I mentioned. We each tried to do our work, take care of our brief, and not to look into anything that anyone else was doing, anyone else that we perhaps happened to be in touch with in our work. If there was a request for assistance, obviously, we would rush to one another's aid, but we weren't exactly used to exchanging information among ourselves, in terms of our respective briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] [In English] Again, I hear the translation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't even hear any translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, please slow down, because there is a slight delay with the French interpretation. The second thing, I have a question to put to the witness. Here's my question: Witness, in your answer to Judge Moloto's question, you said that, officially, in September 1994, you learned, during a morning briefing session, for the first time, about the existence of the Mujahedin. How did you learn it during this meeting? What was discussed during the briefing session? How was the information conveyed to you, officially speaking, because you said it's during that briefing session that you were officially informed of the existence of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on this subject, when I learned officially in my service about the presence and existence of that category of persons in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, specifically in the area of responsibility of the corps to which I belonged, that is, the 3rd Corps, it is true it happened at one of the morning briefings that I had to attend and that were held in my sector every day. My chief, Major Osman Vlajcic, had materials that he received from the superior service, the superior commander, that is, the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps. He commented on them, and he signed off various documents. We called it "signing off," meaning indicating on each document which operative is going to deal with it. I believe there was one report that contained information about some activities of the Mujahedin, "the Mujahid Detachment," I believe it was called. I mean, I'm trying to be as accurate as I can after all this time. I'm afraid I can hardly remember very precisely after all this time how it was formulated, but I am trying to be as precise in answering your question as I can. Let's see if I will succeed. So he, who was in charge of that area, said he had some information. That's when I learned about their existence and the fact that their activities are monitored, but I had no further interest in that because I had my own desk, my own brief, and my own work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, I noted that you told us that your commander, Major Osman Vlajcic, received the information from the superior command in the 3rd Corps about the Mujahedin, and I would be curious to know, if you know, whether he had also received information from the 35th Division; that is to say, from underneath. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I have explained already the hierarchy in my prior testimony to the best of my ability, considering that I am not a military person myself. I believe, and I suppose, that the communication went like this: The security organ of the 35th Division forwarded information to the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps. The latter evaluated the contents of that information and evaluated the subjects; and depending on that, he directed it to various sectors of the security -- military security service. That included our sector of counter-intelligence. I believe that's how the communication went within our service; that is, within our sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you ever encounter any Mujahedin during your work as an operative in the counter-intelligence sector?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not myself, because there was no need for me to meet any of them. My boss was in charge of that area of work. I worked exclusively with prisoners of war from the side of the Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor, and I was involved in operative work in the field, gathering information that was relevant to the units involved in combat activities in the area of 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, we're going to be looking at some documents in a minute. If the Mujahedin or El Mujahedin Detachment took prisoners, would this not put you in contact with them?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, because in the chain of command and control, I was the last person to do the actual work; that is, the interview with the prisoner of war, regardless of whether he was captured by the Mujahedin or some other unit in the area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you told us that one of your sources of information, sir, was interviews with prisoners of war. You told us this, this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I said is correct. I did talk to each of the prisoners who were brought to the Zenica Reception Centre for Prisoners of War, but only once they were brought to the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what counsel is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So if there was -- if, for instance, the El Mujahedin had taken prisoners in their custody, were they under the same obligation to transport the prisoners to the POW centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wonder if this question -- I'm objecting. I'm just wondering if this question could be clarified a little. It was put: "Would the El Mujahedin be under the same obligation to transport the prisoners to the reception Centre in Zenica." I don't believe the witness has explained any obligation to transport prisoners, certainly not at any length, and I think it would be useful to establish that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will go along with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, what were the normal procedures in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps for when a prisoner of war was captured? Who would take custody of the prisoner, and where would the prisoner go?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did describe the procedure briefly in my prior testimony. The unit conducting some combat activities in a particular area of responsibility, if it captures one or more prisoners of war, had the obligation to take such prisoners of war to the Reception Centre in Zenica as soon as practicable. I'm talking about the procedure that I knew of as an operative of the counter-intelligence sector. Now, what really happened in the field, I cannot know that firsthand, because I have never been in the field. I spent all my time in my office in Zenica; and when such prisoners of war were brought to Zenica, I could interview them in the centre, not in the field. But I said that's the way I suppose it should have happened. It was supposed to work that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And was there a particular unit that did the physical transporting of the prisoners to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, within the Command of the 3rd Corps, we had a battalion of the military police; and within that battalion, there were a number of organisational units. I believe that members of that MP battalion, maybe not the battalion itself but one of its subordinate units, had the obligation to physically transport prisoners of war from the place where they were captured, from the unit that captured them, to the centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So I'll go back to my original question, which is: When -- if the Mujahedin or if the El Mujahedin Detachment had taken custody of POWs, were they under -- were they required to follow the same procedures as anyone else within the area of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, from all I know, they were supposed to. Whether they really followed the procedure or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document -- Exhibit 553, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, while waiting for the English version to come up, sir, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, as far as I can see - the top part of the copy is not so good - this seems to be a report resulting from an interview with prisoners of war from -- this is really illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can the English version be moved up so that the Chamber can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you some specific questions, sir: Can you tell us whether this document is from the 35th Division, military security service department, to the 3rd Corps commander, security service department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us if the date of this document is the 22nd of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat. The copy is very bad, especially when important details are concerned, but I believe that is, indeed, the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you see the subject matter, which shows an interview was carried out; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see that. It's an interview with POWs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. There's something wrong with the screen right now. There is something wrong. Okay. Okay. I don't have -- okay. Sorry. Could you turn to the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, do you see, sir, in the second -- the second line of the body of the document, it says, "the interview was carried out in the Reception Centre in the village of Livade." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the Reception Centre in the village of Livade is located?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't tell you. I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know who conducted these interviews at the Reception Centre in Livade?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose the interviews were conducted by one of the members of the security service; that is, one of the members of the military security service of the 35th Division. If I see any initials, I could perhaps say who exactly. Initials are usually in the bottom left corner; but, no, there are none. But it was certainly one of the members of that security service of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And given the fact of your position as operative in the counter-intelligence, and your area of responsibility was Serb and Montenegro aggressors, having received this information at the 3rd Corps level, would you have received -- shouldn't you have received or did you receive this information immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before -- sorry to interrupt. Before asking whether he received the information immediately, could we please ascertain whether the witness received this document at all or has ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When is the first time that you learned of these POWs?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we move the document a bit. That's excellent. Here, we see the date the document was created, 22nd July 1995, and I see the mark, the sign-off that I spoke about earlier. Every document received by the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps would be reviewed by the assistant commander; and based on the contents, he would direct it to a particular person or sub-sector in the service. What we see here is that it was directed to the sector to which I belonged, and the mark says that a report should be made. The specific task was given by the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Alihodzic. It says that "Sare," that was my nickname, "Sare should talk to the Muslims." Can I clarify that, if you want me to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. During combat operations, two or three prisoners of war were taken -- two, three. Three. It's a bad copy. However, in addition to those three prisoners of war who were Serbs, and I believe one was Ukrainian, around 11 Muslims were captured, and those Muslims either fought or worked in so-called "labour platoons" for the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we are going to get into that in a bit. My question to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt. Can we please zoom in a little bit on the English version, so that we can see what the parties are talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My specific question to you, Mr. Saric, is this: You say that you were tasked with interviewing these POWs. This report is dated the 22nd of July. So when did you interview the POWs, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you that with any certainty. There's probably a document, some written trace of it, maybe an Official Note, or a report about the interview with the said persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And we will look at those documents, but would there -- is there any indication from this document why these -- whether or not these prisoners were going to be transported to Zenica in accordance with the standard procedures?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it written here that they would be transported, but I believe that they were eventually transported to Zenica, to the Reception Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you say "eventually," do you know how long after this document it was that they were transported to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely, but I believe there is a document that will confirm the time when I conducted an interview with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My last question, before I move on to another document, is: Do you know of any reason why they would not have been immediately transported to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said something about that, briefly. The unit that took one or more prisoners in the course of combat, security organs would probably immediately talk to those prisoners because the information that they are able to provide at that moment is topical and priceless at that moment. If I may finish, the information that they would give three days later is worthless.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. So it would be important for you, as the counter-intelligent operative in the 3rd Corps, to speak with them as soon as possible, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, but I could not wield any influence on that. I would interview them when they arrived at the POW Reception Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. This document may be put away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a few questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember - before we put away that document, please, can we bring it back - do you remember at any time interviewing these POWs that are mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at the names, I believe I did interview them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember when you interviewed them, the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hardly. I could hardly remember the exact date, but I believe I talked to them within 10, 15, maximum a month, after reading this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember where you interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the prisoners of war that I interviewed were interviewed exclusively in the POW Reception Centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may the witness be shown P02303. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us if this document is dated the 23rd of July, and it's from the 3rd Corps security service department to the General Staff Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if we could look at the bottom of the document in B/C/S, and the second page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the initials -- who "GI" is?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page in English, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, does this document -- does this document again contain the subject matter of the prisoners that were taken in July?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, in fact, if we can move the document down a little bit in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In fact, the three names, there are three names mentioned, are those the three names mentioned from the previous document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this document also mentions 11 enemy troops in the first sentence. Can you tell us what those -- who those are?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are 11 persons who were Muslims, Bosniaks, who were used by the Serb-Montenegrin aggressor to perform labour on fortifying the combat positions and lines of the Serb-Montenegrin aggressor. We call these "labour platoons."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from the first -- the first paragraph of the document, it mentions that these prisoners had been interviewed. My question to you is: Were these interviews conducted by you or anyone in the 3rd Corps, or were these interviews -- are you reporting to the Main Staff about interviews that had been conducted by someone in the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make one thing clear. I'm not the person who produced this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson. Just a second, sir, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's last answer is touching upon the very reason that I stood up. It hasn't been established that this witness has ever seen this document before. His initials are not on it. We can see the date of the document, and the witness has just told the Trial Chamber the time period that he believes that he spoke to the persons mentioned in this report. So I don't believe it's appropriate for the witness to be asked about whether he conducted the interview with the prisoners that's mentioned in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection. He understands the content of the document. All I'm asking is whether this report was a result of any interviews conducted by his department, or are they just reporting on what someone else did. He would know, being in the counter-intelligence department of the 3rd Corps military security service, whether he interviewed them and whether these interviews resulted in this report. It's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I find a little incomprehensible from the objection is that a little earlier I asked the witness if he did remember ever interviewing at least these three, and he said, "Yes, some 10, 15, maximum a month," after he saw the previous document. Now, the last part of Mr. Robson's argument is: "It is not appropriate for the witness to be asked about whether he conducted the interview with the prisoner that's mentioned in this particular document." I don't understand that because he's already told us that he conducted those interviews anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was drawing the Trial Chamber's attention to the date on the face of this document; and from the last document that we saw, that mentioned information about when the three men, prisoners of war mentioned in this document, were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. These documents are a day apart: The one was the 22nd, the other one was the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this gentleman said he did interview these three some 10, 15, maximum a month, after he saw the document of the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So to say it is inappropriate to ask him whether he did interview these people, that's what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to spend more time on this document than necessary because there are other documents, but I guess I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Why would there be a document, a second document, about the same subject matter the day after the first document? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the heading of this document. Is it not so, Madam Sartorio, that the document of the 22nd was a report from the 35th Division to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that this one is from the 3rd Corps to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I stand corrected, so let me just -- let me just wrap up this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is there a stamp on this document, sir, that indicates that it was received by the General Staff [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a stamp which shows that the document was received. It's an incoming stamp. It was received by the General Staff of the Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So, in line with what Mr. President just said, and in line with the previous document, can you tell us whether this is just reporting up what your department had received the previous day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It's not an objection; it's a matter to do with the record. The witness, at line 6 of page 26, stated: "It was received by the General Staff Security Administration of the Army. The words "Security Administration" have not be captured in the transcript. I just wonder if that could be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's recorded now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That could be added in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, it went to the General Staff of the Army Military Security Administration; correct? Could you answer "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Defence's submission that a sufficient basis has not been laid to admit the document into evidence. There's not a link, we would submit. This is a document that went from the 3rd Corps security service department, which is -- although the witness is within the 3rd Corps, we've heard that there were layers within the security service department. It went to the Military Security Administration of the General Staff. The witness has said that he did not see this document, and all he's been really done -- all that's been done is that he's been asked to read out segments of it. We can see from the document that the author of the document is Ekrem Alihodzic. He will be coming to testify next week. So in my submission, Your Honour, it's not appropriate for the document to be admitted through this witness. It can be dealt with in due course by the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, given documents that have come in, he is completely familiar with the substance of the document. This is his department that he worked for, and he has answered the questions about the document. This is no different than other documents that have come in through witnesses. They don't have to be the author of the document. They don't have to have seen the document previously. If they're aware of the contents, and he was able to answer questions about the content, I would argue that there is a sufficient basis for the admissibility of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This question of admission of documents is really becoming a festering sore. I'm not quite sure. It does seem as if there is an enjoyment of just standing up and objecting to admission of documents at times because maybe people feel uncomfortable about them. You know, I can remember when the last witness that was cross-examined by Madam Vidovic, that a whole lot of documents were being tendered in during that cross-examination which were in exactly the same position as the documents exactly like this. A person looks at the document. He understands and knows the content of the document. He's not the author of the document, but he knows who the author is, can say who the author is, identifies the document, and the document goes in. Now, we now have another standard that you've got to be the author of that document for the document to come in. It's no more a question of Rule 89 (C), which says you admit anything that's got probative value. Now you've got to be the author also. I would like guidance from the parties on just how and what standard is supposed to be used here to admit documents. Is authorship a requirement now? Yes. You're on your feet. I am pointing at you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify, we don't say that authorship is necessary. We're following the -- we're taking it from the guidelines that the Trial Chamber set out at the beginning, and you said there needed to be a sufficient link. The complaint is really that all that's this witness has done is really being asked to read a few extracts from the document, but he's not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like the witness to be led on who wrote the document and whether he knows the person who wrote the document, who signed the document? We can do that. I think you should do that, ma'am, just lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. But just one point, Your Honour. I did ask him what 11 enemy troops meant, and he did explain who they were, so he's obviously is familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the obvious. The objection is he just commented on the content and didn't lay the foundation. You asked him about the initials of the drafter. He didn't ask him about the signatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know, who is the signatory of this document? Whose name is at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You need to show the witness, please, the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Show him the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Whose name is here, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see is "Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic"; to be more precise, Ekrem Hadji Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This person, was he assistant commander for the 3rd Corps Security Service at this time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may just add something, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And that is -- so he was your immediate superior, Mr. Vlajcic's immediate superior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly or -- yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no further questions with regard to the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 858, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This is probably a good time to take a break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May the witness be shown P02321.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, sir, could you tell us who this document -- the document is to and who it's from, and the date of it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could please pull it all the way down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I believe you're looking for -- are you looking for -- actually, I'll go back to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If we could look at the last page in English and the second page in Bosnian, so the witness may see who wrote the document. You'll need to go one more page in B/C/S, sorry, and then one page previous in English, it looks like. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell, from looking at this document, did you write this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the initials, I think I can confirm that I am the author of this document. I can also say that this was information to do with the results of an interview that was conducted with POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know who "RS" is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the initials of the typist. I dictated this and he typed it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't remember. I know who the person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go back to the front of the document, the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, this document is dated the 25th of July, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is there a stamp showing that the General Staff of the Army Military Security Service Administration received this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the incoming stamp that we can see in the header.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, we see, in the first page, the names. Are these the same three persons who were on the previous documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at their names, and I can see that these are the same persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, in the first sentence of the document - if we could scroll over a tad bit in English - in the English version it says: "Results of the interviews conducted with captured aggressor soldiers." Then after, "To the GS ARBiH Security Administration," it says: "In the interview with the captured aggressor's soldiers, the 35th Division of the Army, SVB, military security service learned the following information." So I take it, from that, that this is a report up the General Staff Military Security Service Administration with regard to the 35th Division interviews. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we ask that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this document has been exhibited. We might want to check that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We've double-checked, Your Honour. It may have been admitted under a different ERN; but under this PT number, our records show it has not been admitted as a document. It's not to say that a duplicate hasn't been admitted, but we would -- if Defence knows, perhaps it could give us the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we'll do our best to check this. I am highly certain that this document was tendered with one of the previous witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The -- one thing that can happen, Your Honour, is the same documents are obtained from different sources, and the other document may not have the stamp, so I would like this document admitted with the stamp. So I'd just ask that it be assigned an exhibit number today; and if we find a duplicate, then perhaps it can be corrected later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Would that be okay with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 859, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness now be shown P03022, and if we could -- if we could go to the last -- the next-to-the-last page in English. Again, we're looking for the signature page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us whether you wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the initials indicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And may we go back, then, to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And would you agree this document is dated the 25th of July, 1995, and it's to the army General Staff, Administration of Military Security? Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what this document is all about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to keep this as brief and accurate as possible. You see, in my evidence today, I've mentioned already that during the fighting, a number of Muslims were captured. Through interviews, we ascertained that these people had been members of the labour platoons. These were Muslims who were captured as members of this labour platoon. They were performing labour for the purposes of the Republika Srpska Army units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is this report written as a result of any interviews that you conducted of these persons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether these 11 Muslim work platoon -- or labour platoon persons were captured at the same time as the other three, Mr. Sikanic and Mr. Trivicevic, that are the subject matter of previous documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was one of the operations carried out by I don't know exactly which unit of the BH Army. It was during that operation that these 11 persons, plus these three POWs, were captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So by the 25th of July, you had interviewed some or all of the 11 persons at -- was this at KP Dom, Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ask that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do, I just want to ask the witness just one question. Witness, you say at line 23: "I think this was one of the operations carried out by I don't know exactly which unit of the BH Army." Do I understand you to say that in your drafting of this document, you didn't establish which unit had captured these labour platoon people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, this may have been an omission on my part. However, at the time, what I found incomparably more important was to find out whatever was of interest to my units. Well, I didn't mean to say "my units," in the sense of units belonging to me, but units that were active and were performing combat operations in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 860, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May now the witness be shown Exhibit 552, please, and if we could scroll down to, again, the bottom to see the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell, from looking at this document, whether you wrote -- are you the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copy is not very clear. But judging by the initials and the signature, I think that I was the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now may we go to the front, the first page again of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So this is dated the 26th of August, 1995. Can you tell us -- can you identify what the contents are of this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the name of this document, you see that it is an Official Note containing the information regarding an interview that was conducted with a POW. You can see the name right there: Velibor Trivicevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you interview this person on the same day that you wrote this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see that the Official Note was produced on the 25th, which was right after the interview. There's a possibility that perhaps I talked to this person a day earlier or perhaps on that same day, but the time gap between the dates could not possibly have been greater than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are you able to explain to the Chamber why you didn't interview this person until around the 26th of August, yet you interviewed the Muslim work platoon around the 25th? Can you explain why that was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In my evidence, I have already pointed out, and I reiterate that, that my sole task or mission was to speak to POWs the moment they were brought into the Zenica POW Reception Centre, probably the same minute they were brought in. If there was a room that was available, as soon as this POW was brought in, I would receive instructions from my boss to the effect that the prisoner was there, and I would receive an order to go there, right there and then, and talk to this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And just to clarify the record, when I asked you about interviewing the Muslim work platoon around the 25th, I meant the 25th of July. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you make any inquiry about the three soldiers who had not appeared or been brought to Zenica? Did you want to speak with these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But to avoid all misunderstanding, I did not make any inquiries about them, nor was I interested, until the moment these persons would arrive to the POW Reception Centre. I had no time and no possibility to do such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May this document be put away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask of this witness beforehand. Witness, please, you spoke of "Odbrana Republike." What does it mean? Were you talking about the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you say that again? I'm not sure I got the right interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, at the beginning of the document, on the right-hand side, we can read "Odbrana Republike," which has been translated into English as "National Defence." I was wondering if this was referring to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, that is the mark of confidentiality of a document. This "National Defence" means "military secret." It's the degree of confidentiality of a document. This document is considered to be strictly confidential, because it contains strictly confidential information we received from that person. If you ask me if that's the Ministry of Defence, well, yes, the General Staff had above it the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sign, this mark at the beginning of the document, doesn't correspond to the institution which received the document in this case? Madam Sartorio, could you try and clarify this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, when you made this Official Note, where did this Official Note go to, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Official Note was first reviewed by my immediate superior, Major Osman Vlajcic. He evaluated the quality and volume of information contained therein. After his personal assessment, he would decide whether there was any need to make a report of that information to be sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was that decision ever made or was it not made, to send this document to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have a question before we admit this. At page 37, line 14, Madam Sartorio asked the question: "Now, did you make any inquiry about the three soldiers who had not appeared or been brought to Zenica? Did you want to speak with these soldiers?" Your answer was: "No. But to avoid all misunderstanding, I didn't make any inquiries about them, nor was I interested, until the moment these persons would arrive to the POW Reception Centre. I had no time and no possibility to do such things." I'm not quite sure I know which three soldiers are being spoken about here. I know that we have spoken about three soldiers and 11 labour platoon people. Now, those three soldiers that we spoke about included this person. Now, when the question says,"Did you make any inquiry about the three soldiers who had not appeared," I would like to know which soldiers these are. Are you able to tell us, Witness, because you answered the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very possible that this is one of them, and that is easily verifiable. We had a document a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: When you answered, "No," which three soldiers did you have in mind which you didn't interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Prosecutor asked me a question referring to the three prisoners who were captured together with the 11 Muslims from the labour platoon. On one document those three persons are listed first before the reference to the 11 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this one that you are talking about on this Official Note is one of those three. So the question should have been: "Did you talk to the other two," but it says "the other three." I want to know, who did you have in mind. Madam Sartorio, are you able to clear this for us, because I don't know who you're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Your Honour. Actually, the question was about the time period between the time when they were captured - and we saw some documents earlier - which was the 21st of July, and the time of the interview of this person, which was around the 28th of August. My question to him was whether he had tried to interview them during that month period, and that was my specific question with regard to this. Well, Mr. Sikanic is the subject matter of this, as well as the other two, which are mentioned in several of the previous documents. But I can go back to those documents, and we can put the names on the record, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, I had been under the impression that when we were dealing with or when you were dealing with Exhibit 553 and Exhibit 858, the witness told us that he did interview those people around those -- I'm not quite sure. I think I asked you the question: "When did you interview these people and where you interviewed them?"" In your answer, you said, "10, 15, up to a maximum of a month, after they had been arrested." Now, did you also interview the other two -- or let me rephrase my question. Is it your testimony, sir, that this one, Velibor Trivicevic, did you interview him; or let me ask you, on what date did you interview him, if you did interview him at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt, but we have a document to show that, that I'm getting to next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you see, you have been mentioning dates of interviews, and I'm trying to clear the dates. We're talking about the 26th August, 28th August, 25th July, and I'm trying to find out exactly when these people were interviewed, because a number of dates have been given, mainly by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think the dates are in the documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we need to go back. If we could put Exhibit 859, please, and we'll go to the signature page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you need the signature page? It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, you wrote this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. What is the contents of this document about? What, specifically, is this about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I created the document and I signed it. On the basis of information we received from security organs of the 35th Division, we informed the security of the General Staff about the interviews with those three POWs. We just forwarded this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And these three POWs, could you, for the record, please state their names?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from this document that the interview was conducted by the military security organ of the 35th Division. The interviewees were Branko Sikanic, Velibor Trivicevic, and Igor Guljevatej.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: Did you, sir, ever interview these people, because now this report talks about an interview by the 35th Division? Did you personally interview these people at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from the moment when those people were brought to the Reception Centre, I talked to them, and that is probably reflected in a document that the Office of the Prosecutor has. But this is an interview with those people that was conducted in a different, lower unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I suggest that you listen to the question that is put, and try to answer the question as briefly as you possibly can. If you can say, "yes," just say, "yes." My question to you is: Did you, at any stage, ever interview these people? "Yes," "No," "I can't remember"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you remember when, on what date, you interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, briefly, can the witness be shown again 860.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the exhibit, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, it's an exhibit. I'm going to clarify everything again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, we talked about this document a moment ago. You wrote this document; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This involves interviews of the 11 Muslim work platoon members; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you, I believe in your testimony, you indicated that you had participated in interviewing these persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I also asked you if these 11 Muslim work platoon members had been captured and detained, along with the three persons that we just mentioned in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the document itself, we see they were captured in combat, so in the same operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, may we go to document 552 now, please -- Exhibit 552, 552. That's not the same one. Well, now, can I have a moment, Your Honour, to double-check the number of the exhibit to show him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me avail myself of this opportunity, while Mrs. Sartorio is looking for something. For the record, I want to say the document that was admitted today under number 859 was admitted earlier, in fact, as Exhibit 595. It's completely identical. It only had a different ERN number. The same is true of document 858 admitted today. It was admitted earlier as 581. I'm sorry, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: With regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic, for that assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, may I be heard? The document that she claims -- that Defence counsel claims is identical does not have the stamp received in by the Main Staff, so it has -- it's a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can check. It is identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, both of you, ladies. Let the documents stay as they are; and if there is any cross-referencing, let's please ask the Registrar to make a cross-reference and that's it. Let the document stay in, the document on the record. Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would like to respond to 858 as well, Your Honour, but perhaps not at this time. Defence counsel says there's another duplicate, but I would like time to look at that duplicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. If what they are suggesting covers 858 as well, 858 and 851 will stay on the record, and we will also ask the Registrar to make a cross-reference between those two. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now may the witness be shown 858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are done with 552, Exhibit 552?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We talked about this document as well, sir. Now, this document, do you agree, in the first sentence, I asked you about the captured 11 enemy troops, and are these the 11 work platoon soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And also contained in the same document below, you will see the name of the three soldiers again: Mr. Sikanic, Trivicevic, and Guljevatej. Those are the same three soldiers from other documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now may the witness be shown PT2446.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, did you write this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a look at the last page. Yes, but this document does not bear my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But that's your name; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my initials, my name. I think I wrote this document, but the signature is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it is your document? You drafted the document, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to the first page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, what is the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of this document, in this Official Note of the security service, resulted from the interview with Branko Sikanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you conduct the interview of Branko Sikanic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you recall when you conducted this interview and if this document can help you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see the heading. It says that this Official Note was done on the 25th of August, 1995; that it was made on the 24th, a day earlier; and that it was made just after the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 861, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness be shown P02485, and may we go to the last page, the signature page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, did you participate in writing this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the initials, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we go to the first page now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So this appears to be an Official Note, and it states it's going to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Staff, Security Administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not an Official Note. This is a report titled: "Information," and it is true it was sent to the Security Service of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is the contents? Can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document speaks of the result of the interview conducted with POW Dusko Pejicic. The copy is not very good, but I believe it was Dusko Pejicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May this document be admitted in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 862, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness now be shown P02487, and go to the second page, the signature line, please.
